igcse-0580-sets-notation.description: List the elements of a set, count distinct members and use Cambridge's Extended membership and subset symbols.

sections.title: How do I turn a rule into a list?
sections.label: Core · List elements
sections.intro: A set groups objects that pass a test. The objects can be numbers, cards or anything else named in the question. A rule after a colon tells you which objects belong.

blocks.html: In \(\{x:x\text{ is an integer},\;-3

figure.alt: Number line. The filled integer points are −2, −1, 0, 1 and 2. The point −3 is open.
figure.caption: The rule allows integers greater than −3 up to and including 2.

blocks.title: How to do it
blocks.html: Read one boundary at a time. A strict sign excludes its endpoint. Write the candidates in order so you can check that every allowed integer is present.

blocks.title: List the integers in a set
blocks.prompt: Write all the elements of \(A=\{x:x\text{ is an integer},\;-6<x\leq 1\}\).
blocks.hint: Look at each boundary sign on its own before writing the list.
blocks.solution:
Read the condition from left to right. Begin at the first integer greater than \(-6\), which is \(-5\).

The sign \(\leq\) includes the upper endpoint \(1\). The set is \(\{-5, -4, -3, -2, -1, 0, 1\}\).

retry.feedback: The strict inequality excludes \(-6\). Start one integer later.
The upper inequality includes \(1\). Add this endpoint.

blocks.html: A list of integers stops at the next integer. If the rule allows all real numbers, the interval contains more than the integers you can list.

blocks.title: List the integers in a set
blocks.prompt: Write all the elements of \(A=\{x:x\text{ is an integer},\;-3<x\leq 4\}\).
blocks.hint: Look at each boundary sign on its own before writing the list.
blocks.solution:
Read the condition from left to right. Begin at the first integer greater than \(-3\), which is \(-2\).

The sign \(\leq\) includes the upper endpoint \(4\). The set is \(\{-2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4\}\).

retry.feedback: The strict inequality excludes \(-3\). Start one integer later.
The upper inequality includes \(4\). Add this endpoint.

sections.title: How do I count the members?
sections.label: Core · Count members
sections.intro: A set may be listed in any order. Each distinct element belongs just once, even if a list repeats it. Compare which entries appear before comparing counts.

blocks.html: \(n(A)\) asks how many distinct elements are in \(A\). It gives a number. A list of the elements gives a set.

blocks.title: How to do it
blocks.html: Cross out repeated copies. Count each remaining entry once and give the count as a number.

blocks.title: Count distinct elements
blocks.hint: Count each distinct element once. The order of the list has no effect.
blocks.solution:
The repeated entry \(30\) is the same element each time. Write the distinct elements as \(\{24, 27, 30\}\).

Count the members of that set. \(n(D)=3\).

retry.feedback: This counts the repeated element twice. Cross out its second appearance before counting.

blocks.html: A set with one member is not the same answer as a count of one. In a question asking for the set, keep the braces even around one entry.

blocks.title: Count distinct elements
blocks.hint: Count each distinct element once. The order of the list has no effect.
blocks.solution:
The repeated entry \(35\) is the same element each time. Write the distinct elements as \(\{27, 30, 33, 35\}\).

Count the members of that set. \(n(D)=4\).

retry.feedback: This counts the repeated element twice. Cross out its second appearance before counting.

sections.title: Extended: Is it a member or a subset?
sections.label: Extended · Membership and subsets
sections.intro: To test membership, look up an individual entry. To test a subset, check every member of a whole set. Use the object on the left of the symbol to decide what kind of test to make.

blocks.html: \(3\in B\) says that the number 3 belongs to \(B\). \(\{3\}\subseteq B\) says that all members of the set \(\{3\}\) are in \(B\). Their negative forms are \(\notin\) and \(\nsubseteq\).

figure.alt: Set A is drawn fully inside B, which is inside the universal set rectangle.
figure.caption: Every member of A also lies in B, so \(A\subseteq B\).

blocks.title: How to do it
blocks.html: One missing element is enough to rule out a subset. The empty set \(\varnothing\) has no members and is a subset of every set. Equal sets are subsets of each other.

blocks.title: Choose the membership symbol
blocks.prompt: Let \(A=\{29,32\}\). Complete \(29\;\square\;A\) with the correct symbol.
blocks.hint: Decide first whether the left side is a single element or a set.
blocks.solution:
The object on the left is the number \(29\), so we need a membership symbol.

The number is in the list. Use \(\in\).

retry.feedback: The subset symbol compares two sets. The number on the left is a single element.
The not-a-subset symbol also compares two sets. Check whether the number belongs to A.

blocks.html: \(\varnothing\) and \(\{0\}\) mean different things. The first set has no elements. The second has one element, the number zero.

blocks.title: Choose the true subset statement
blocks.prompt: Let \(B=\{31,33\}\). Which statement is true?
blocks.hint: A subset can be equal to the set that contains it.
blocks.solution:
Check the members of each candidate set. \(36\) is not in \(B\), so option B is false.

Both \(31\) and \(33\) belong to \(B\). A set is a subset of itself, so C is correct.

retry.feedback: Check every member of the set on the left. \(36\) is absent from \(B\).
The symbol \(\notin\) says that \(33\) is absent. Look for it in the list again.
The set \(B\) has two elements. The empty set has none.

blocks.html: In a written question, label the sets and the universal rectangle. Check every listed element or region against the question.

examples.title: List the integers in a set
examples.question: Write all the elements of \(A=\{x:x\text{ is an integer},\;2<x\leq 9\}\).
solution: Read the condition from left to right. Begin at the first integer greater than \(2\), which is \(3\).
The sign \(\leq\) includes the upper endpoint \(9\). The set is \(\{3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9\}\).

examples.title: List the integers in a set
examples.question: Write all the elements of \(A=\{x:x\text{ is an integer},\;-4<x\leq 3\}\).
solution: Read the condition from left to right. Begin at the first integer greater than \(-4\), which is \(-3\).
The sign \(\leq\) includes the upper endpoint \(3\). The set is \(\{-3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3\}\).

examples.title: Count distinct elements
examples.question: \(D=\{31,23,26,29,31\}\). Find \(n(D)\).
solution: The repeated entry \(31\) is the same element each time. Write the distinct elements as \(\{23, 26, 29, 31\}\).
Count the members of that set. \(n(D)=4\).

examples.title: Count distinct elements

solution: The repeated entry \(32\) is the same element each time. Write the distinct elements as \(\{26, 29, 32\}\).
Count the members of that set. \(n(D)=3\).

examples.title: Choose the membership symbol
examples.question:
Let \(A=\{28,31\}\). Complete \(34\;\square\;A\) with the correct symbol.

A. \(\in\)   B. \(\notin\)   C. \(\subseteq\)   D. \(\nsubseteq\)
solution: The object on the left is the number \(34\), so we need a membership symbol.
The number is absent from the list. Use \(\notin\).

examples.title: Choose the true subset statement
examples.question:
Let \(B=\{30,32\}\). Which statement is true?

A. \(\{30,35\}\subseteq B\)   B. \(\{30,32\}\subseteq B\)   C. \(32\notin B\)   D. \(B=\varnothing\)
solution: Check the members of each candidate set. \(35\) is not in \(B\), so option A is false.
Both \(30\) and \(32\) belong to \(B\). A set is a subset of itself, so B is correct.

revision.body:
Know what the answer represents before you start.

How do I turn a rule into a list?

In \(\{x:x\text{ is an integer},\;-3

Read one boundary at a time. A strict sign excludes its endpoint. Write the candidates in order so you can check that every allowed integer is present.

How do I count the members?

\(n(A)\) asks how many distinct elements are in \(A\). It gives a number. A list of the elements gives a set.

Cross out repeated copies. Count each remaining entry once and give the count as a number.

Extended: Is it a member or a subset?

\(3\in B\) says that the number 3 belongs to \(B\). \(\{3\}\subseteq B\) says that all members of the set \(\{3\}\) are in \(B\). Their negative forms are \(\notin\) and \(\nsubseteq\).

One missing element is enough to rule out a subset. The empty set \(\varnothing\) has no members and is a subset of every set. Equal sets are subsets of each other.
revision.examTip: \(\varnothing\) and \(\{0\}\) mean different things. The first set has no elements. The second has one element, the number zero.

igcse-0580-sets-two-regions.description: Place each element in a two-set Venn diagram and read union, intersection, complement and bracketed expressions.

sections.title: Where does each element go?
sections.label: Core · Draw and intersect
sections.intro: Start with the rectangle, which sets the universe. Each circle stands for one property. An entry has a single position even when it belongs to both circles.

blocks.html: The rectangle represents \(\mathcal{E}\), the universal set. The shared lens represents \(A\cap B\). The corner outside both circles is still part of \(\mathcal{E}\).

figure.alt: Set A on the left and B on the right. The three inside regions are A only, both and B only. Neither is inside the rectangle outside the circles.
figure.caption: Place shared entries in the lens. Every element belongs in exactly one of these four regions.

blocks.title: How to do it
blocks.html: Place shared entries in the lens first. Then fill the A-only and B-only parts. Every remaining entry in the universe belongs outside both circles. If the sets have no shared entries, they are called disjoint.

blocks.title: Find the entries in the overlap
blocks.prompt:
The universal set \(\mathcal{E}\) contains the integers from \(39\) to \(46\), inclusive.

\(A\) = \(\{40, 42, 44, 46\}\) and \(B\) = \(\{41, 44, 45, 46\}\).

List the elements of \(A\cap B\).
blocks.hint: Test each number against both sets. Keep it only if both tests pass.
blocks.solution:
Compare each entry in \(A\) with the list for \(B\).

Only \(\{44, 46\}\) appears in both lists. Write these elements once in the overlap.

retry.feedback: The union includes both circles. For the intersection use only the shared lens.
These entries are in A only. The overlap contains entries in both A and B.

blocks.html: A shared number appears once in the lens. Writing it separately in A and B creates two copies of one element.

blocks.title: Decide whether sets overlap
blocks.hint: Look for a shared entry. On Arena you can type ‘empty’ if there are none.
blocks.solution:
All entries of A are even. All entries of B are odd. No entry belongs to both.

There is no overlap, so the intersection is \(\varnothing\). Its size is zero.

retry.feedback: This is the union. To enter the intersection, keep only elements appearing in both lists.

sections.title: Which regions belong to ‘A or B’?
sections.label: Core · Read the union
sections.intro: In set notation, ‘or’ includes the case where both descriptions are true. To find the union, follow the outer edges of the two circles.

blocks.html: \(A\cup B\) includes A only, both and B only. \(A\cap B\) includes the overlap only.

figure.alt: Both circles are shaded all the way through the overlap. The outside region is unshaded.
figure.caption: The blue area includes both circles and their overlap. It represents \(A\cup B\).

blocks.title: How to do it
blocks.html: Take every entry in at least one circle. Make a single list and check that a shared entry appears only once.

blocks.title: List the union
blocks.prompt:
The universal set \(\mathcal{E}\) contains the integers from \(43\) to \(50\), inclusive.

\(A\) = \(\{43, 45, 47, 48\}\) and \(B\) = \(\{44, 45, 48, 49\}\).

List the elements of \(A\cup B\).
blocks.hint: Here ‘or’ includes entries that are in both sets.
blocks.solution:
Take the elements in \(A\) then add any elements of \(B\) that do not appear in that list.

Include the shared elements once. \(A\cup B\) is \(\{43, 44, 45, 47, 48, 49\}\).

retry.feedback: Include the overlap as well. The union is everything in either circle.
The overlap is part of the union. Add the A-only and B-only entries.

blocks.html: If the question says ‘exactly one’, leave the lens out. If it says ‘at least one’, include the lens.

blocks.title: List the union
blocks.prompt:
The universal set \(\mathcal{E}\) contains the integers from \(46\) to \(53\), inclusive.

\(A\) = \(\{46, 48, 50, 51\}\) and \(B\) = \(\{47, 48, 51, 52\}\).

List the elements of \(A\cup B\).
blocks.hint: Here ‘or’ includes entries that are in both sets.
blocks.solution:
Take the elements in \(A\) then add any elements of \(B\) that do not appear in that list.

Include the shared elements once. \(A\cup B\) is \(\{46, 47, 48, 50, 51, 52\}\).

retry.feedback: Include the overlap as well. The union is everything in either circle.
The overlap is part of the union. Add the A-only and B-only entries.

sections.title: How do I find the complement?
sections.label: Core · Find complements
sections.intro: A complement keeps the elements excluded by a named set, within the chosen rectangle. Changing the universal set can change the complement even if a circle keeps the same entries.

blocks.html: \(A'\) contains everything in \(\mathcal{E}\) outside \(A\). That includes the B-only part and the space outside both circles.

figure.alt: The amber shaded region is the part of the rectangle outside circle A. This includes B only and the area outside both circles.
figure.caption: The complement \(A'\) is outside A and inside the rectangle.

blocks.title: How to do it
blocks.html: Trace the boundary of A. Keep every entry within the rectangle but outside that boundary. Reject entries in the lens because they are inside A.

blocks.title: Find a complement
blocks.prompt:
The universal set \(\mathcal{E}\) contains the integers from \(47\) to \(54\), inclusive.

\(A\) = \(\{47, 49, 51, 53\}\) and \(B\) = \(\{47, 50, 52, 53\}\).

List the elements of \(A′\).
blocks.hint: Look at every region in the rectangle outside the A boundary.
blocks.solution:
Start with every element in \(\mathcal{E}\). Cross out those inside \(A\), including its overlap with \(B\).

The remaining B-only and outside entries form \(\{48, 50, 52, 54\}\).

retry.feedback: Include the region outside both circles, because it is also outside A.
The B-only region lies outside A. Include those entries too.

blocks.html: A complement is tied to its rectangle. Do not write numbers or objects that were never in the universal set.

blocks.title: Find a complement
blocks.prompt:
The universal set \(\mathcal{E}\) contains the integers from \(50\) to \(57\), inclusive.

\(A\) = \(\{50, 52, 54, 56\}\) and \(B\) = \(\{50, 53, 55, 56\}\).

List the elements of \(A′\).
blocks.hint: Look at every region in the rectangle outside the A boundary.
blocks.solution:
Start with every element in \(\mathcal{E}\). Cross out those inside \(A\), including its overlap with \(B\).

The remaining B-only and outside entries form \(\{51, 53, 55, 57\}\).

retry.feedback: Include the region outside both circles, because it is also outside A.
The B-only region lies outside A. Include those entries too.

sections.title: Extended: What do the brackets change?
sections.label: Extended · Combine regions
sections.intro: Do the inner operation first. A prime on an entire bracket reverses membership of the whole bracketed region. Compare this with putting the prime on just one circle.

blocks.html: \((A\cup B)'=A'\cap B'\) is outside both circles. \((A\cap B)'=A'\cup B'\) is everything except the lens.

blocks.title: How to do it
blocks.html: Sketch the region named in brackets, then keep the rest of the rectangle. To represent ‘A only’ directly use \(A\cap B'\).

blocks.title: Find the complement of the union
blocks.prompt:
The universal set \(\mathcal{E}\) contains the integers from \(51\) to \(58\), inclusive.

\(A\) = \(\{52, 54, 56, 58\}\) and \(B\) = \(\{53, 56, 57, 58\}\).

List the elements of \((A\cup B)\prime\).
blocks.hint: The prime outside the brackets applies to the whole union.
blocks.solution:
Work inside the brackets first. \(A\cup B\) contains \(\{52, 53, 54, 56, 57, 58\}\).

Remove all of these from the rectangle. The elements outside both circles are \(\{51, 55\}\).

retry.feedback: Both circles were in the brackets. Remove B-only entries as well as the entire A circle.
This is the set inside the brackets. Now take its complement.

blocks.html: Look at what the prime touches. A prime after a closing bracket acts on everything in the brackets.

blocks.title: Find the complement of the union
blocks.prompt:
The universal set \(\mathcal{E}\) contains the integers from \(54\) to \(61\), inclusive.

\(A\) = \(\{55, 57, 59, 61\}\) and \(B\) = \(\{56, 59, 60, 61\}\).

List the elements of \((A\cup B)\prime\).
blocks.hint: The prime outside the brackets applies to the whole union.
blocks.solution:
Work inside the brackets first. \(A\cup B\) contains \(\{55, 56, 57, 59, 60, 61\}\).

Remove all of these from the rectangle. The elements outside both circles are \(\{54, 58\}\).

retry.feedback: Both circles were in the brackets. Remove B-only entries as well as the entire A circle.
This is the set inside the brackets. Now take its complement.

revision.body:
Read a region, then check what the set operation asks for.

Where does each element go?

The rectangle represents \(\mathcal{E}\), the universal set. The shared lens represents \(A\cap B\). The corner outside both circles is still part of \(\mathcal{E}\).

Place shared entries in the lens first. Then fill the A-only and B-only parts. Every remaining entry in the universe belongs outside both circles. If the sets have no shared entries, they are called disjoint.

Which regions belong to ‘A or B’?

\(A\cup B\) includes A only, both and B only. \(A\cap B\) includes the overlap only.

Take every entry in at least one circle. Make a single list and check that a shared entry appears only once.

How do I find the complement?

\(A'\) contains everything in \(\mathcal{E}\) outside \(A\). That includes the B-only part and the space outside both circles.

Trace the boundary of A. Keep every entry within the rectangle but outside that boundary. Reject entries in the lens because they are inside A.

Extended: What do the brackets change?

\((A\cup B)'=A'\cap B'\) is outside both circles. \((A\cap B)'=A'\cup B'\) is everything except the lens.

Sketch the region named in brackets, then keep the rest of the rectangle. To represent ‘A only’ directly use \(A\cap B'\).
revision.checks: • A shared entry appears once in the lens.
revision.examTip: Look at what the prime touches. A prime after a closing bracket acts on everything in the brackets.

sections.title: Do the numbers name entries or count them?
sections.label: Core · Read region counts
sections.intro: A list of song numbers inside a circle shows which songs meet a rule. A single region value in a survey can stand for several people. Read the context before doing any arithmetic.

blocks.html: With counts, add the numbers in the requested regions. Each person, response or object belongs to one region.

sections.title: Why do whole-circle totals double-count?

blocks.title: Recover the outside count
blocks.prompt:
A record of library loans groups the entries into \(A\) for a graphic novel and \(B\) for an audiobook.

There are 22 entries altogether. \(n(A)=7\), \(n(B)=14\) and 2 entries belong to both sets.

How many entries belong to neither set?
blocks.hint: The circle totals include the overlap. Find the number in the union before finding neither.
blocks.solution:
Adding the whole circles gives \(7+14=21\). This counts the 2 shared entries twice.

Subtract the overlap once. The union contains \(21-2=19\) entries.

Subtract the union from the total to find neither. \(22-19=3\).

retry.feedback: The circle totals double-count those in both. Subtract the overlap once before finding neither.

blocks.html: The given value of n(A) belongs to all of the A circle. Putting it into A only and then adding the lens changes the stated circle total.

igcse-0580-sets-three-regions.description: Use all eight regions of a three-set diagram, reconstruct pair-only counts and combine operations in the correct order.

sections.title: Where are the eight regions?
sections.label: Extended · Read eight regions
sections.intro: Three sets give eight possible membership patterns. Each entry can be inside or outside each of the three circles. The centre belongs to all three.

blocks.html: Exactly two gives the three pair-only regions. At least two also includes the centre. None of the sets contains the outside region.

figure.alt: Region counts: A only 4, B only 5, C only 6, A and B only 3, A and C only 2, B and C only 6, all three 1 and outside all 8.
figure.caption: Exactly two includes the three counts \(3,2,6\). At least two also includes the centre, whose count is 1.

blocks.title: How to do it
blocks.html: Name a region before entering a value. Use one circle label for an exclusive single region, two labels for a pair-only region, and all three for the centre.

blocks.title: Count entries in exactly two sets

B and C only2

How many entries are in exactly two sets?
blocks.hint: Exactly two rules out the centre. At least two would include it.
blocks.solution:
Use the three regions labelled ‘and … only’. Exclude the central region because those entries are in three sets.

Add those regions: \(3+5+2=10\).

retry.feedback: You included the centre. Remove the entries in all three sets.

The 14 entries in \(A\cap C\) include those in \(B\) as well.

Remove the centre once. The pair-only count is \(14-5=9\).

extraPractice.title: Recover a pair-only region
extraPractice.prompt:
A community centre lists sessions. Sets \(A\), \(B\) and \(C\) record entries for bouldering, printmaking and coding, in that order.

\(n(A\cap C)=16\). There are 7 entries in all three sets.

Find the number of entries in both \(A\) and \(C\), but outside \(B\).
extraPractice.hint: A pair intersection includes the triple intersection. Remove it to find the pair-only region.
extraPractice.solution:
The 16 entries in \(A\cap C\) include those in \(B\) as well.

Remove the centre once. The pair-only count is \(16-7=9\).

retry.feedback: The pair total includes the centre. Subtract the entries in all three sets.

revision.body:
Fill the three-set diagram from the centre outwards.

Where are the eight regions?

Exactly two gives the three pair-only regions. At least two also includes the centre. None of the sets contains the outside region.

Name a region before entering a value. Use one circle label for an exclusive single region, two labels for a pair-only region, and all three for the centre.

Why start with the triple intersection?

\(n(A\cap C\cap B')=n(A\cap C)-n(A\cap B\cap C)\). The same method works for the other pairs.

Complete the three pair-only regions next. In each whole circle, subtract its two pair-only regions and the centre to get only that circle. Fill the outside last.

How do I read a longer expression?

For \((A\cup B)\cap C\), first allow A or B. Keep only regions inside C. The centre passes both tests.

Mark the eligible regions with a finger or a little tick. Compare each region with the whole expression before adding counts. If a whole bracket has a prime, keep precisely the other regions.
revision.checks: • Exactly two excludes the centre. At least two includes it.
revision.examTip: C only passes the C test. It fails the A-or-B test, so leave it out of the expression above.
